messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Children Crying): Kids crying, Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Name Reminders: Hearing related names
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping, Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
  Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me, Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ren Thongchai is a 40-year-old Thai-American journalist, divorced, who presents for his initial intake following a referral from his primary care physician. He had spent the better part of his career covering political unrest across Southeast Asia, a vocation he had chosen out of genuine conviction that bearing witness mattered. That conviction was tested irrevocably three years ago when, while reporting on a crackdown near the Thai-Myanmar border, he was detained by paramilitary forces and held for eleven days. During that time he was subjected to repeated sessions of physical and psychological torture — beaten, deprived of sleep, subjected to prolonged stress positions, and at intervals made to listen to the sounds of other detainees, including children separated from their families in the same facility, crying in adjacent rooms. He was eventually released without explanation and made his way back to Bangkok, then to the United States. He has told almost no one the full account of what happened.

In the months that followed his return, Ren found that the memory of those eleven days did not arrange itself into anything he could hold steadily in his mind. When he tried to deliberately recall the sequence of events — to write about it, to explain it to a therapist he briefly saw — he found the memory strangely inaccessible, as though it had been placed behind frosted glass. There were entire periods he simply could not retrieve, gaps that troubled him not because he feared what they contained but because their blankness felt like evidence of something broken in him. What he could access felt so extreme, so discontinuous from the person he had been before, that he had come to half-believe it had not happened to him at all — or had happened to someone who no longer existed.

He had returned to journalism in a diminished capacity, writing domestic policy pieces from a desk in Chicago. The newsroom, which had once felt like home, became a place of vigilance. He found himself watching colleagues closely — tracking the shift of a body, the tone of a voice — certain in a way he could not fully articulate that harm could arrive without warning from almost anyone. Ordinary sounds in the open-plan office made him flinch visibly, and he had begun positioning himself near exits. One afternoon, a junior reporter's young daughter was brought in during a school holiday; the child began crying when she scraped her knee, and Ren left the building without a word and did not return that day. His editor noticed the pattern of absences. A story he had been assigned on immigration detention — work that would once have felt urgent and meaningful — sat unfinished on his desktop for four months.

Outside work, Ren had progressively withdrawn from the friends and colleagues he had known before the detention. He had come to believe, with a quiet but absolute certainty, that people who had known him before could see something in him now — some mark of what had been done to him, or of what he had done or failed to do — and that their company confirmed it. He was certain there was something fundamentally wrong with him as a person, not merely something that had happened to him. He had acted in ways during those eleven days that he measured against the man he had believed himself to be and found the distance unbearable. He did not specify the details in intake, but the guilt and shame he described were not abstract. He had also largely stopped eating regular meals, managing on very little, in a pattern he could not entirely explain except that appetite had come to feel irrelevant or undeserved.

He spent considerable time, particularly at night, turning over the question of what he could have taken differently — a different route, a different source, an earlier departure — dwelling on the architecture of prevention until the early hours. Occasionally, hearing a name phonetically similar to one of the guards, spoken casually in a café or on the radio, produced a sudden wave of dizziness that he found deeply disorienting and that he had come to dread.

What finally brought Ren to seek help was his divorce being finalised last month — a quiet administrative event that nonetheless made the isolation feel total. He arrives hoping, tentatively, to understand why he cannot simply move forward. What he is most afraid of is being seen clearly.
